paragraphs.text: Hypohidrotic/tooth/nail type ectodermal dysplasia-19 (ECTD19) is an ectodermal dysplasia with oligodontia, hypo- or anhidrosis with absent sweat glands, recurrent skin abscesses resembling hidradenitis suppurativa, poikiloderma, nail dysplasia, and bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment (Schneider et al., 2026). Natal teeth and sparse hair are seen in some patients. Unlike Van der Woude syndrome and popliteal pterygium syndrome, which are also caused by IRF6 mutations, the disorder does not include cleft lip/palate or lip pits (Schneider et al., 2026).

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) gave full phenotypic data on the 2 previously reported patients (P1 and P2), unrelated male teenagers aged 17 and 14 years. Both had natal teeth on their first day of life. These teeth were weakly anchored and were lost spontaneously or extracted in early infancy. P1 later developed 7 deciduous teeth with some delay and 12 permanent teeth, 2 of which were removed. Most of his teeth had enamel defects and enamel hypomineralization. Oligodontia had left the alveolar crest of his lower jaw highly atrophic. P2 developed only 9 permanent teeth. From early infancy, both patients had episodes of overheating and difficulty regulating body temperature. Both had recurrent skin abscesses, especially in the genital/gluteal area, behind the ears, in the armpits, and in the mouth. Their skin was very dry, with plantar hyperkeratosis and, in winter, blistering on the backs of the toes. Testing showed anhidrosis, and confocal laser scanning microscopy found no sweat glands on the palms. Some toenails and fingernails were dysplastic, thickened, or deformed, with distal onycholysis. Other features were increased thick mucus in the nose and upper throat and dry cerumen. Both had bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment since infancy, treated with hearing aids. Submucous cleft palate was excluded in both. P1 also had a tendency to allergies, including several anaphylactic reactions to milk protein.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) also described a 22-year-old woman (P3) who was referred for anhidrosis, dry skin, and intolerance of environmental temperatures above 22 degrees C. She had diffuse xerosis and dilated follicular ostia. She had had several episodes of skin abscesses mimicking hidradenitis suppurativa in the groins, axillae, and intergluteal fold, treated with antibiotics and surgery. Her scalp hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes were normal. She had pincer nails on both big toes and bilateral acquired sensorineural hearing loss. No natal teeth were remembered. Her lips and palate were normal. She reported epistaxis, crusted rhinitis, and insufficient salivation. She had bilateral superficial punctate keratitis with a reduced tear film break-up time. Her tooth eruption was delayed, and she had 16 persisting deciduous teeth and only 2 permanent teeth. The authors found a shared pattern of tooth agenesis in P1, P2, and P3. All 3 had permanent upper incisors but no mandibular incisors or canines and no permanent premolars. Skin histology in P1 and P3 showed focal subcorneal clefting and basal spongiosis, and sweat glands were absent in both.

paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated boys with ECTD19 (P1 and P2), Schneider et al. (2026) identified the same heterozygous c.653T-A transversion in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene, resulting in an ile218-to-asn (I218N) substitution. P1 was studied by high-throughput sequencing, and Sanger sequencing of the parents confirmed that the mutation was de novo. In P2, Sanger sequencing of IRF6 was done after no pathogenic variants had been found in EDA, EDAR, EDARADD, or TP63. The parents' DNA showed no change at this position, so the mutation was considered de novo. In a 22-year-old woman with ECTD19 (P3), whose parents were nonconsanguineous and healthy, trio whole-genome sequencing found a heterozygous de novo c.658T-C transition in IRF6, resulting in a ser220-to-pro (S220P) substitution. The variant allele frequency of 30.5% indicated mosaicism. The authors noted that in silico analyses supported pathogenicity but that the variant was ultimately classified as of unknown significance.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) noted that the ECTD19 mutations are amino acid changes in exon 6 of IRF6. This exon encodes a region of unknown function between the DNA-binding and protein-binding domains. By contrast, IRF6 missense mutations causing Van der Woude syndrome and popliteal pterygium syndrome are found mostly in exons 3, 4, 7, 8, and 9. Because none of the 5 patients had impaired palatal development, the authors concluded that p.Ile218Asn, p.Ser220Pro, and p.Ile218_Ser220delinsSerSerGlyAla do not limit DNA binding of the mutant protein, at least in the fusing palatal shelves. They cautioned that cleft lip/palate could not be ruled out in other patients with similar mutations.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) stained skin for IRF6. Keratinocyte nuclei from P1, who carried I218N, stained more strongly than control nuclei. Nuclear staining in the epidermis of P3, who carried S220P, was more patchy, consistent with mosaicism. Keratin-17 staining was normal. In an AlphaFold3 structural model, both point mutations affected a short alpha-helix at the end of the region of unknown function. The authors proposed that the disorder arises through a gain-of-function mechanism, with increased IRF6 activity. They speculated that the hearing impairment and the abscesses resembling hidradenitis suppurativa may result from disruption of the IRF6-p63 regulatory loop. They also noted that Zhang et al. (2026) had suggested a gain-of-function effect of the ile218 substitutions.

paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated male teenagers with ECTD19 and natal teeth, Schneider et al. (2026) identified a heterozygous c.653T-A transversion in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene, resulting in an ile218-to-asn (I218N) substitution. The mutation was predicted to be deleterious. It was de novo in both patients, since neither patient's parents carried a change at this position. Keratinocyte nuclei in the skin of 1 patient showed stronger IRF6 staining than controls. Schneider et al. (2026) also noted that the same substitution had been found in 1 of the 2 patients described by Zhang et al. (2026).

paragraphs.text: In a 22-year-old woman with ECTD19 (P3) and nonconsanguineous healthy parents, Schneider et al. (2026) used trio whole-genome sequencing to identify a heterozygous de novo c.658T-C transition in the IRF6 gene, resulting in a ser220-to-pro (S220P) substitution. The variant allele frequency was 30.5%, indicating mosaicism, and her skin showed patchy nuclear IRF6 staining. In silico analyses supported pathogenicity, but the variant was ultimately classified as of unknown significance.

agent.process_note: I read the full text of Schneider et al. (2026) in full. For Peschel et al. (2025) and Zhang et al. (2026) only the titles were available. Details about the patients and variants in those two papers therefore come only from Schneider et al.'s account of them (2 unrelated patients with I218N; P4 with p.Ile218_Ser220delinsSerSerGlyAla and P5 with I218N). I could not find the nucleotide change for the delins variant, so I did not list it as an allelic variant. No reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no IRF6 MIM number or cytogenetic band. Chromosome 1 comes from the genomic coordinate (chr1) given by Schneider et al. The papers do not use the term 'autosomal dominant'. The AD inheritance listed rests on heterozygous de novo occurrence.
